Maladaptive Strategies.value: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

vignette: Lina, a 20-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married soldier, has been grappling with the aftermath of an assault that left her feeling disconnected from both herself and her community. The traumatic event itself occurred in the barracks where she was stationed. One night, as she was working late on a report, a fellow soldier broke into her room, assaulting her despite her pleas for him to stop. Lina has vivid visual memories of this event — images that replay like a video in her mind. However, these memories often feel alien, as if they belong to someone else rather than herself. The extremity of the assault makes it hard for her to believe she was actually involved. The memory of this traumatic night keeps intruding on Lina’s daily life. She finds herself constantly redirecting her thoughts to other things or trying to make sense of what happened by overanalysing every detail, which only intensifies the memories’ vividness and frequency. These intrusive recollections have led Lina to engage in maladaptive strategies like overeating as a way to distract herself from the distressing images. Lina’s belief that somebody else would have intervened to stop the assault has deeply impacted her sense of self-worth and competence, leading to feelings of guilt and inadequacy. This negative appraisal makes it harder for her to cope with everyday situations, pushing her towards further maladaptive behaviors such as overeating or trying to drown out the memories by constantly thinking about something else. Over time, these coping mechanisms have led Lina to experience a growing sense of disconnection from herself and her community. The more she turns to food and redirection as ways to cope, the less she feels like she can connect with others in meaningful ways. She is certain that the person she has become since the assault is unrecognizable to her, contributing to an even deeper sense of isolation. The alienation from her culture and community has also grown as Lina withdraws into herself. Her once strong connection to her South Eastern Asian heritage now feels distant and tenuous, further exacerbating her negative appraisals about her own worth and ability to cope with the trauma she experienced. Lina’s daily life as a soldier is now fraught with triggers that remind her of the assault. The barracks where it happened are constantly in her mind, making it difficult for her to perform her duties without being overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts and memories. Her overanalysing has only made these images more vivid and distressing, creating a cycle that feels almost impossible to break. The combination of her maladaptive coping strategies and the persistence of traumatic memories has left Lina feeling increasingly disconnected from herself and others. She is most afraid of never recovering her sense of self and losing all connection to her community. What finally brought her to seek help was the realization that she could no longer function effectively in her role as a soldier, nor find peace within herself. Lina hopes for a way to reconnect with her true self and find healthier ways to manage her distressing memories without feeling like she is living in isolation from those around her. She wants to reclaim a sense of control over her life and feel like the person she was before the assault once again.
